results.title: Standardized Data Protocols → Term
results.content:
Title: Standardized Data Protocols → Term
The conceptual roots of standardized sustainability data protocols extend deep into several intellectual traditions. The contemporary importance of standardized data protocols in sustainability discourse cannot be overstated; it has shifted from a niche concern to a central pillar of global economic and policy deliberation. Supply chain transparency demands, driven by consumer awareness and regulations concerning human rights and environmental impacts (like deforestation-free products), also necessitate standardized data exchange across complex value chains. The pathway toward robust, standardized sustainability data protocols has been marked by incremental steps, punctuated by significant conceptual shifts and the emergence of influential frameworks. Several pivotal shifts characterize the evolution of standardized sustainability data protocols. The quest for effective standardized sustainability data protocols is a dynamic field, characterized by continuous innovation in tools, methodologies, and conceptual frameworks. Despite progress, significant barriers impede the universal adoption and effectiveness of standardized sustainability data protocols:. Standardized Data Protocols in the sustainability context represent far more than mere technical specifications for reporting; they embody a fundamental shift in how organizations perceive, measure, and communicate their interactions with the wider world. Within the social dimension, standardized data protocols aim to bring visibility and comparability to issues often obscured within complex organizational structures and global value chains. Finally, concepts like impact valuation attempt to directly integrate environmental and social performance (measured via standardized protocols) into economic calculations, challenging traditional GDP-focused metrics and potentially reshaping economic incentives. Numerous instances highlight the positive impact of applying standardized sustainability data protocols:. These lessons underscore the need for critical engagement with standardized data, recognizing its limitations, continuously refining protocols and assurance practices, and ensuring the pursuit of standardization serves, rather than subverts, genuine sustainability objectives. The significance of Standardized Data Protocols in the sustainability domain transcends mere technical compliance; it resides in their fundamental role as enablers of systemic change and navigators of complexity. Currently, standardized sustainability data protocols are at a critical juncture, characterized by accelerating adoption, increasing regulatory convergence, yet persistent practical challenges. The future trajectory of standardized sustainability data protocols points towards greater integration, technological enablement, and an expanding scope, though not without navigating significant complexities.

results.title: Time horizons and discount rates in Swedish environmental policy: Who decides and on what grounds? - ScienceDirect
results.content:
Title: Time horizons and discount rates in Swedish environmental policy: Who decides and on what grounds? - ScienceDirect
# Time horizons and discount rates in Swedish environmental policy: Who decides and on what grounds? We analyse the time horizons/discount rates used in Swedish environmental policy. Interviews with Swedish authorities reveal large variations in the time horizons and discount rates used in their policy decisions. We suggest that there may be a need for co-ordination and, possibly, harmonization, of the choices of time horizons and discount rates. In this study, we critically analyse the time horizons and discount rates used in Swedish environmental policy. Based on these interviews we identify the time horizons and discount rates used in Swedish environmental policy and explore the justifications given for their adoption. Our data reveal large differences in the discount rates and time horizons used. While some of the differences between the time horizons and discount rates of different environmental policy areas may be justified, the differences appear to be unsystematic and in many cases insufficiently justified. In Section 6 we address the further issues whether the lack of consistency in the use of time horizons and discount rates presents a problem to environmental decision-making and whether one could justifiably ask for greater coordination and, possibly, harmonization, of the choices of time horizons and discount rates. Below, the information gained in the interviews is summarized under headings referring to *time horizons* (Section 4.1–4.2) and *discount rates* (Section 4.3–4.4). The widespread adoption of insufficiently justified time horizons and discount rates in the Swedish public sector indicates a general need for overview and, possibly, revision. After interviewing Swedish policymakers about this issue – discount rates and time horizons in particular – authors concluded that at present the choice of discount rates in national environmental policy is “uncoordinated, insufficiently justified, insufficiently transparent, and therefore not politically accountable” (ibid, p. In summary, we recommend using a value not higher than 4–5% for the social discount rate for the European countries as well as to include an exhaustive portfolio of hurdle rates for all the technologies included in the energy optimisation model. Recent debates over the social discount rate also concern the question of why different government agencies of the same country use different discount rates (Hansson et al., 2015).
